claims.claim: A raster image is built from a rectangular grid of small colored squares called pixels (picture elements); the pixel is the basic unit of a raster image, and a computer records color data per pixel.

Pixel dimensions (the count of pixels across the width and height, e.g. 3000 x 2400) are a fixed property of a raster file, whereas resolution is a density: how many of those pixels are packed into each linear inch when the image is displayed or printed. A pixel is fundamentally a sample with no inherent physical size; it acquires a size and a density only when the image is displayed, printed, or scanned at a given ppi.

PPI (pixels per inch) measures the pixel density of an image or an electronic display, while DPI (dots per inch) properly measures the density of the ink or toner dots a printer lays down; a printer translates image pixels into a pattern of dots (for example via halftone screening or dithering), so ppi and dpi are related but distinct quantities that are frequently used loosely as synonyms.

Roughly 300 ppi is the working convention for high-quality print because commercial presses screen photographs into halftone dots at about 200 to 300 dots per inch, and the practical rule of thumb delivers pixels at about twice the halftone line ruling (Required PPI = 2 x LPI at final size, so 175 lpi needs about 350 ppi). Around 300 ppi also matches the limit of what the unaided eye resolves at a normal reading distance.

The legacy '72 ppi' screen figure comes from the typographic convention of 72 points per inch and the original 1984 Macintosh, whose display was about 72 pixels per inch so that one on-screen pixel mapped to one typographic point and text appeared on screen at the same size it would print (early WYSIWYG). The 72 ppi assumption persisted in software long after hardware changed, and modern screens have far higher pixel density, with Retina/HiDPI displays commonly exceeding 200-320+ ppi so individual pixels are not discernible at normal viewing distance.

Because print size equals pixel dimension divided by resolution, the same fixed-pixel image printed at a lower ppi spreads its pixels over a larger area: it prints bigger but coarser, with each pixel occupying more physical space. A 3000 x 2400 px image is 10 x 8 inches at 300 ppi but 20 x 16 inches at 150 ppi.

Enlarging a raster image by resampling forces the software to generate new pixels it never captured; interpolation (nearest-neighbor, bilinear, bicubic, and similar) estimates those values from neighboring pixels rather than recovering true detail, so upscaling cannot add real information and introduces blur, softened edges, or jagged/ringing artifacts. Repurposing a low-resolution screen image (for example 72 ppi) for large print therefore looks soft because the file simply lacks the data the output needs.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'ppi' and 'dpi' are genuinely different or interchangeable terms.
positions: Precise/technical usage: ppi is image or display pixel density; dpi is printer dot density, a different physical quantity connected to ppi through screening.
Casual industry usage: 'dpi' is routinely used to label the resolution field of an image (e.g. '300 dpi image'), treating the two as synonyms.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the precise distinction (pixels for images/displays, dots for the printer), then notes that the two terms are widely blurred in practice so learners recognize '300 dpi image' when they meet it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 72 ppi is a meaningful standard for today's screens.
positions: Historical fact: the original Macintosh display was about 72 ppi, tied to 72 points per inch.
Common misconception: web images 'must' be saved at 72 ppi, or that all screens are 72 ppi today.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents 72 ppi as a historical origin that stuck in software, and states plainly that modern displays have much higher device-pixel density (Retina/HiDPI), so for on-screen use it is the pixel dimensions, not a stored ppi tag, that matter.

sourceRecords.title: Pixel density
sourceRecords.notes: Read to support: ppi (and ppcm) measures the pixel density of an electronic image device; a printer translates pixels into a series of dots via dithering, distinguishing printer dots from display pixels; a pixel has no inherent size or unit (it is a sample) but gains a physical size and a density only when printed, displayed, or scanned; the unaided human eye generally cannot differentiate detail beyond about 300 ppi (viewing-distance dependent); and modern displays reach very high densities (hundreds of ppi). Reference-only; facts synthesized, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: About Points and Pixels as Units
sourceRecords.notes: Read to support the origin of the 72 ppi figure: there are 72 points in one inch in both PostScript and CSS; the original Macintosh had a 512x384, roughly 72 ppi display and the OS used that value to map physical measurements to pixels so a typographic point equaled one screen pixel, producing genuine WYSIWYG; the 72 ppi assumption then stuck in software even as later displays reached higher densities (e.g. 91-98 ppi on later Macs), while Windows assumed 96 ppi. Reference-only technical article; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Image scaling
sourceRecords.notes: Read to support: enlarging a raster image requires generating a new image with a higher pixel count, so new pixel values must be created; interpolation methods (nearest-neighbor, bilinear, bicubic, Fourier) estimate those values and each introduces characteristic artifacts (jaggedness, reduced contrast/blur, ringing); upsampling cannot recover truly lost detail because the new pixels are calculated approximations, not captured data. Reference-only; facts synthesized, no wording reproduced.
